Hi Marissa —

Thanks for the recap and for sending the draft. High level: yes, the targets are what we had in mind. A few clarifications from our side before Legal spends cycles on redlines: 

1) Latency measurement: we care most about p95 end-to-end latency as seen by our users (i.e., time from our client request hitting our edge -> first token visible to user). If there’s a difference between time-to-first-token vs time-to-last-token for long streaming responses, we’d prefer the SLA focus on time-to-first-token for initial responsiveness, with optional guidance for streaming tail latency.

2) Exclusions: Scheduled maintenance is expected; we need clear thresholds (e.g., notifications >72 hours prior, and a monthly maintenance cap). Also want explicit exclusions for incidents caused by our misconfiguration or network outside Redwood’s managed network.

3) Reporting cadence: Monthly SLA report is fine, but we’ll need access to raw per-route latency histograms for at least 90 days for our internal audits.

4) Remedies: service credits are OK, but we want to understand the escalation path and whether there’s an on-call engagement for production-impacting regressions.

Couple of smaller asks:
- For streaming, confirm that Redwood supports token-by-token flushes and that the measurement for p95 time-to-first-token excludes the initial TLS handshake and DNS resolution when possible.
- We expect you to document regional differences (us vs eu) if the measurement differs.

If you can get Dev to confirm measurement definitions and the exclusions language, Legal can take a first pass on the draft this week.

—Emily

Hi all —

Thanks — dug into the telemetry and here are proposed, implementation-aligned language snippets you can drop into the SLA draft. I kept them non-binding and operationally realistic.

1) Latency measurement (recommended SLA language):
"Latency for text-generation APIs is measured as the 95th percentile (p95) of time-to-first-byte (TTFB) aggregated per-customer and per-route over the monthly reporting window. Time-to-first-byte is defined as the interval between Redwood's edge accepting an authenticated request and the first byte of model output leaving Redwood's serving layer. Where possible, client-side network operations such as DNS resolution and TLS handshake are excluded from the SLA measurement; metrics in the Console will show both edge-to-first-byte and end-to-end (client-observed) latency for diagnostic purposes."

Notes: Our edge logs capture request accept timestamps and first-output timestamps. For streaming responses we record first-output per request. TTFB p95 is stable across regions for identical instance classes; minor regional variance will be surfaced in the monthly report.

2) Exclusions (recommended SLA language):
"SLA measurements and availability calculations will exclude: (a) scheduled maintenance windows with prior notification of at least 72 hours and a monthly cap of 6 hours unless otherwise agreed; (b) incidents caused by customer configuration changes or misuse; (c) third-party network outages outside Redwood's control; and (d) force majeure events. Redwood will make commercially reasonable efforts to provide advanced notice of maintenance and coordinate timing with the customer to minimize impact."

3) Reporting and access (recommended SLA language):
"Redwood will provide a monthly SLA report that includes per-route p50/p95/p99 latency statistics, availability metrics, and incident summaries. Upon request, Redwood will provide raw per-route latency histograms (JSON or CSV) with 90 days retention for audit purposes. Access will be via the Redwood Console and an authenticated S3/Drive export link as mutually agreed."

4) Remedies & escalation (summary):
- Monthly service credits tiered to the degree of SLA breach (example table in attached draft).
- Incident escalation: initial acknowledgment within 30 minutes for Sev-1 production impacting incidents; on-call engagement per the enterprise support schedule in the contract.

Open/considerations:
- If Acme requires end-to-end client-observed SLA (including last-mile), we can provide reporting but it has higher variance due to customer network; recommend keeping contractual SLA on edge-to-first-byte and reporting both metrics.
- For streaming tail latency we'll add guidance (non-contractual) on best-effort optimizations (batching limits, chunk sizes, model tokenization effects).

I attached a quick screenshot of the per-route histogram export (perf-metrics-screenshot.png) showing p95 calc. If this looks good I can paste the exact text into ACME-SLA-DRAFT-v2.pdf and send to Legal.
